source: Wang et al. (2022) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning
finding: Share of sampled paths that agree with the final voted answer is strongly tied to accuracy on GSM8K. Authors say low agreement can flag low confidence.
numbers: Figure 5 on GSM8K (plot only, no coefficient in the text). Imperfect-CoT prompt on LaMDA-137B: greedy 17.1 to 14.9, self-consistency recovers.
quote: consistency ... is highly correlated with accuracy
limits: Plot only. Mean trend, not per-item. Says nothing about items where all paths agree and are wrong.
agent_relevance: Cluster share of the top answer is a free, cheap gate on multi-step reasoning (gap 4). Pair it with a check for consistent-wrong cases.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Let's sample step by step: Adaptive-Consistency
finding: Compared stop rules for sampling answers: BETA (Bayesian stability of the leader), ENTROPY, MAJORITY, RANDOM. BETA beats ENTROPY and MAJORITY at equal average sample cost. MAJORITY mostly underperforms BETA and ENTROPY. RANDOM is worst.
numbers: 17 datasets, 3 LMs. Cost cut 4.4x GPT-3.5-turbo (accuracy 76.4 vs 76.2), 1.9x Vicuna-13B (54.0 vs 54.1), 3.4x code-davinci-002 (69.7 vs 69.8). Up to 7.9x with no loss. At 10 average samples on GSM8K, Adaptive-Consistency is about 3 points above plain self-consistency.
quote: reduces the computational budget by 7.9 times
limits: Stop rules over final answers on closed-form tasks (math, commonsense). Not probe-choice stops. A raw entropy threshold is worse than the Bayesian stability test.
agent_relevance: Best direct comparison of stop rules found (gap 5): a posterior-stability test beats a raw entropy threshold. Use for sample-then-stop gates; not tested on EIG stops.

source: Li et al. (2024) Escape sky-high cost: Early-stopping self-consistency (ESC)
finding: Stop sampling when all answers in a small window agree (answer entropy zero). Distributions whose top answer is correct have much lower entropy than those whose top answer is wrong.
numbers: Sampling cut: MATH -33.8%, GSM8K -80.1%, StrategyQA -76.8%, CommonsenseQA -78.5%, Coin Flip -84.2%, Last Letters -67.4%, comparable accuracy. Window 5 (8 for MATH); averaged over 10 runs.
quote: distributions with correct one as highest probability answer typically have much lower entropy
limits: Zero-entropy window is the strictest threshold. Hard task (MATH) saves least.
agent_relevance: Supports an entropy-zero stop rule for answer sampling (gap 5). Savings shrink on hard items, exactly where budget matters.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Hypothesis Search: inductive reasoning with language models
finding: On 100 random ARC tasks with GPT-4, generating language hypotheses, filtering them, then writing programs beats direct prompting. Coverage caps the result: the model produced a correct hypothesis for only 49 of 100 tasks.
numbers: Direct 17%; Program Only (64 programs, no hypotheses) 23%; Summarized Hypo. (64 hypotheses summarised to 8, 8 programs each, 3 feedback rounds) 30%; Human-selected 33%; Human-written (LARC) 45%; Icecuber DSL search 43%. Of 30 solved by summarised hypotheses, 28 had a correct hypothesis before summarising. 33 of 49 tasks with a correct hypothesis got a correct program (67%). CoT without programs 19%.
limits: Top-1 accuracy, GPT-4-0314, n=100. Compute not matched: hypothesis arms use 64 hypotheses plus 64 programs plus execution feedback. Program Only is the closest match (64 programs).
agent_relevance: Closest evidence for gaps 1 and 2 on ARC: inventing and filtering hypotheses helps (17 to 30) but only where a correct hypothesis is among the candidates (coverage 49%). The hypothesis list, not the scoring, is the bottleneck.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just ask for calibration
finding: For RLHF chat models, confidence stated in words is better calibrated than token probabilities or sampled label agreement on TriviaQA, SciQ, TruthfulQA. Asking for several guesses with probabilities helps further.
numbers: Expected calibration error cut by a relative 50% (abstract) for ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude. Label-probability estimate used n=10 samples; n=20 gave no meaningful gain.
quote: verbalized confidences emitted as output tokens are typically better-calibrated than the model's conditional probabilities
limits: Factual QA only. Calibration is bin-level, not item-level correctness on multi-step reasoning. Claude-2 conditional probabilities were weaker than GPT and Claude-1.
agent_relevance: Item-level uncertainty for a closed API model (gaps 6, 8): ask for probabilities over several candidates, do not rely on logprobs. Still untested on ARC-style items.

source: Piriyakulkij, Kuleshov, Ellis (2024) Active preference inference using language models and probabilistic reasoning
finding: LLM defines the probabilistic model by prompting; the question is chosen to minimise expected posterior entropy. Authors show expected entropy minimisation equals expected model change maximisation in their setup (the cross-entropy term is constant over questions).
numbers: Web-shopping preference task; 8 candidate questions sampled; entropy-reduction LLM beats vanilla instruction-tuned and ReAct baselines after about four questions; example expected-entropy scores 1.80, 1.61, 1.98 for three candidate questions.
limits: Simplified shopping simulator. Does not test probability gain.
agent_relevance: Second independent EIG-for-LLM result outside 20 Questions (gap 1). Two natural scores collapse into one, so no need to choose between them. Probability gain still untested (gap 3).

source: Choi et al. (2025) BED-LLM, appendix F.3: static vs history-updated likelihood
finding: Letting the answer likelihood depend on the whole dialogue history lowered success in most cells versus a static likelihood. Authors blame context-induced calibration shifts.
numbers: 20 Questions, 5 models x 3 datasets = 15 cells, n=100 each. Static beat updated in 13 of 15 (Animals GPT-4o 93 vs 86, Qwen 95 vs 89; Celebrities Qwen 84 vs 70, Llama-70B 55 vs 44; Things GPT-4o 64 vs 57). Updated won in 2 (Animals Llama-8B 67 vs 63, Llama-70B 80 vs 79). SE 2.2-5.0.
limits: Standard errors overlap in many single cells; the 13-of-15 count is the stronger signal. Only 20 Questions.
agent_relevance: Gaps 6 and 7: carrying full history into the probability prompt hurt. Keep the likelihood prompt short and fixed; put history only into the belief set.

source: Choi et al. (2025) BED-LLM Table 1 discussion: Entropy vs Split vs Implicit Maximization
finding: A non-deterministic likelihood mainly buys a proper EIG, not a better marginal entropy. Asking the model to pick the most informative of the same candidate questions (Implicit Maximization) beat Prompt-Only at far lower cost.
numbers: Entropy ablation slightly better than Split; full BED-LLM above all ablations. Implicit Maximization above Prompt-Only (values in Table 1; run times in Table 3).
limits: No equal-token comparison in the passage read. Implicit Maximization shares BED-LLM's filtered belief set.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 2: a cheap middle option exists (LLM judges best question among candidates from a filtered belief set). Test it first at equal tokens before paying for full EIG.

source: Choi et al. (2025) BED-LLM appendix A: expected likelihood entropy (ice cream vs film genre)
finding: Predictive entropy of the answer alone prefers noisy questions (ice-cream flavour has high answer entropy but says nothing about film taste). Full EIG subtracts the expected likelihood entropy. Deterministic-likelihood methods cannot do this.
numbers: Entropy without subtraction was the strongest ablation but still below full EIG (K13: Animals 88 vs 79 mini, 93 vs 88 4o).
limits: This is about noisy answers, not about the estimation error of p(y|h).
agent_relevance: Gap 6 partly closed: the failure mode is known and cheap to avoid (subtract answer noise). Accuracy of p(y|h) itself is not measured in anything I opened.

source: Li, Kim, Wang (2025) QuestBench: can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information in reasoning tasks?
finding: Underspecified reasoning problems where one missing variable blocks the answer; the model must pick the right clarifying question. Strong on arithmetic, weak on logic and planning. Solving the full problem does not imply asking the right question.
numbers: Abstract: best models 40-50% on Logic-Q and Planning-Q, near ceiling on GSM-Q and GSME-Q (e.g. GPT-4o zero-shot GSME-Q 99.34%, GSM-Q 92.01%). Accuracy falls with backward search depth, variables and constraints (Spearman, significant for most LLMs on Logic-Q). Models: GPT-4o, o1-preview, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro/Flash, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking, Gemma 2.
quote: models struggle to identify the right question even when they can solve the fully specified version
limits: Multiple choice of questions, one missing variable. No EIG scoring tested; a BFS baseline is included. Table 2 layout garbled in extraction, so only abstract and a few cells quoted.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: on logic and planning, unaided probe choice is weak. Supports an explicit search over hypotheses for the probe step rather than trusting model intuition.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just ask for calibration: Tables 1 and 2
finding: gpt-3.5-turbo and gpt-4 verbalised probabilities are better calibrated than model probabilities, even after temperature scaling.
numbers: Captions of Table 1 (gpt-3.5-turbo) and Table 2 (gpt-4). Cell values not read reliably from extracted columns.
quote: directly verbalizing a probability ... yields significantly better-calibrated confidence estimates
limits: Cell values not usable from the extraction.
agent_relevance: Same as d05; direction confirmed for two models.

source: Hoffmann et al. (2022) Chinchilla: unit of irreducible loss E (derived check)
finding: The paper calls E the entropy of natural text but I found no unit in the text. Natural log is implied: predicted loss at 70B params and 1.4T tokens is 1.69 + 406.4/N^0.34 + 410.7/D^0.28, about 1.94, which is about 2.80 bits per token, or about 0.70 bits per byte at roughly 4 bytes per token. Chinchilla reports about 0.667 bits per byte on The Pile.
numbers: E = 1.69 nats = 2.44 bits per token (my conversion). Fit: A=406.4, B=410.7, exponents 0.34 and 0.28. The calculation and the 4 bytes per token are mine.
limits: Unit inferred, not stated. Different data (MassiveText vs Pile) and tokeniser. E is a fit floor over all text, not a bound for any task.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: floor is about 2.4 bits per token for web-like text. It is not a bound for structured puzzle answers; do not use it to cap probe gain.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Adaptive-Consistency: speed of stop rules
finding: Dirichlet and Chinese-restaurant-process stop rules perform like BETA at fixed cost but are about four orders of magnitude slower in the stop check.
numbers: BETA check about 4 orders faster than DIRICHLET and CRP; RANDOM worst.
limits: Stop-check time is small next to LLM inference, so speed alone is not decisive.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: the simple Beta test is enough as a stop rule on samples.

source: Fu et al. (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Uses token-level entropy and confidence of reasoning traces to drop low-confidence traces and to stop early once vote share reaches a threshold. Authors report a failure mode: aggressive filtering can hurt when the model is confidently wrong.
numbers: GPT-OSS-120B AIME 2025: DeepConf@512 99.9% vs cons@512 97.0% vs pass@1 91.8%. Online mode cuts generated tokens by up to 84.7% at equal or better accuracy. With 10% filter: DeepSeek-8B AIME25 82.3 to 87.4; Qwen3-32B AIME24 85.3 to 90.8. Averages over 64 repetitions. Benchmarks AIME 2024/25, HMMT 2025, BRUMO25, GPQA-Diamond.
quote: overconfidence on incorrect problems, as seen with GPT-OSS-120B
limits: Needs open logits; semantic entropy not tested. Authors name high-confidence wrong paths as the main limitation. Stricter filter (90%) is safer.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 5: an entropy or confidence gate does work on multi-step reasoning with large token savings, but confident-wrong cases pass; use a conservative setting.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know: item-level use
finding: Item-level self-evaluation (p(True)) is the existing item-level proxy. Model-level log-loss linkage (Huang 2024) is a different thing. No paper I opened tests per-item log-loss or compression as a correctness proxy for an agent's own multi-step answers.
numbers: See evidence_a for numbers. Usable item-level signals found: verbalised probability (d05), agreement share (d01), p(True).
limits: Absence finding; broad search was not possible (WebSearch budget exhausted).
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open for log-loss; use agreement share or verbalised probability as the item-level signal.

source: Oaksford and Chater (1994) rarity-assumption model; Cover and King (1978): attempt to verify
finding: Could not open primary or review text on the rarity-assumption model, its replications, or failed replications. The Wikipedia page cites Oaksford and Chater (1994) only in a footnote with no figures. The Springer page redirected to a login.
numbers: None obtained. Wikipedia: in Wason's original task not even 10% found the correct solution.
limits: This line records a failed access, not a finding.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open. Do not cite figures for K25 or the rarity model beyond what evidence_a and evidence_b hold.
